groups.title: Fastify Fundamentals
groups.question: Walk through how Fastify handles a request from the moment it arrives until the response is sent.

followUps.Request Lifecycle & Hooks: What goes wrong if you put an auth check in the wrong lifecycle hook?
followUps.Schema-Based Validation & Serialization: Why do response schemas make Fastify faster, not just safer?

evidence.text: A request passes through set hooks in order, such as onRequest, preParsing, preValidation, preHandler, the handler, then onSend and onResponse.
Auth belongs in an early hook like onRequest or preHandler, so unauthorized requests are stopped before the handler or expensive work runs.
Putting it in a late hook like onSend means the handler has already run and may have changed data.

notEnough: Only listing hook names without explaining their order or why it matters.

evidence.text: Request schemas validate input before the handler runs, rejecting invalid requests with a 400.
Response schemas let Fastify compile a fast serializer, which is quicker than generic JSON.stringify.
Fields not in the response schema are dropped, so internal data like password hashes isn't sent by mistake.

notEnough: Only saying schemas validate data without mentioning serialization.

groups.title: Plugin Architecture
groups.question: Explain how Fastify plugins organize and share code across an application.

followUps.Plugin Encapsulation with fastify-plugin: Why might a decorator registered in one plugin be missing in another, and how do you fix it?
followUps.Decorators for Dependency Injection: How do decorators make route handlers easier to unit test?

evidence.text: Each plugin gets its own encapsulated context; decorators and hooks it registers are visible only to it and its children.
So a decorator added in one plugin isn't available in a sibling plugin.
Wrapping the plugin with fastify-plugin skips encapsulation and shares its decorators with the parent scope.

notEnough: Only saying plugins organize code without explaining encapsulation.

evidence.text: Decorators attach shared things, like a database client, to the Fastify instance or the request.
Handlers use those injected dependencies instead of importing them directly.
In tests you register a fake version of the decorator, so handlers can be tested without a real database.

notEnough: Only saying decorators add properties without explaining how they help testing.

groups.title: REST API Design
groups.question: Explain how you design a clean REST API that clients can rely on.

followUps.RESTful Resource Modeling: Why should URLs name resources instead of actions, and what does that give you?
followUps.HTTP Status Codes & Error Responses: What breaks when an API returns status 200 for every error?

evidence.text: URLs name resources, like /orders/42, and the HTTP method says the action.
Clients can then guess endpoints, and methods carry known behavior, like GET being safe to repeat and cacheable.

notEnough: Only listing HTTP methods without explaining resources.

misconceptions.text: Says PUT and PATCH do the same thing.

evidence.text: Status codes tell clients what happened: 2xx success, 4xx a client problem, 5xx a server problem.
Returning 200 for errors breaks clients, caches, retries and monitoring that rely on the code.
Error responses should use one consistent body shape, so clients handle them the same way everywhere.

notEnough: Only listing code numbers without explaining why they matter to clients.

groups.title: Project Structure
groups.question: Explain how you structure a Fastify project so it stays healthy as it grows and runs in production.

followUps.Scalable Fastify Project Layout: How would you split a growing Fastify app into folders, and what problem does that solve?
followUps.Graceful Shutdown in Fastify: What happens to in-flight requests during a deploy if the app ignores SIGTERM?

evidence.text: Code is split into folders by feature or layer, such as routes, plugins, services and schemas, rather than one growing file.
Each part then has a clear home, so changes stay local and the app is easier to test and navigate.

notEnough: Only saying split it into folders without explaining how or what it solves.

evidence.text: On deploy, the platform sends SIGTERM before killing the process.
The app should stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, and close database connections, which fastify.close() handles.
Ignoring SIGTERM means the process is killed mid-request, so users get errors and work can be half-finished.

notEnough: Only saying handle SIGTERM without saying what the app should do.
